answers.question: How does ventilation air flow speed affect flame spread and extinction over thin solid materials such as PMMA and cotton-fiberglass fabric in microgravity?

observed.text: In actual-flight microgravity BASS/BASS-II tests of concurrent-flow SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric, the combined dataset varied flow from 40 cm/s down to 1 cm/s and ambient oxygen from 21% to 16%; it reports low-speed quenching limits between 1 and 5 cm/s, with higher quenching speed at lower oxygen. This finding applies jointly to BASS and BASS-II, not BASS-II alone.

For that fabric work, a small flame at low flow allowed observation of ignition, growth, steady spread in some cases, and decay; the BASS-II report describes reducing flow during tests to determine quenching limits.

The query-specific PMMA records are not a matched fabric-flow series: BASS-II-B1 was a 0.1 mm PMMA film at 5 cm/s opposed flow, where sustained spread was observed at 2.2 mm/s before the operator shut off flow; BASS-II-B3 was a 0.1 mm PMMA film at 2 cm/s opposed flow, with no numeric spread rate reported.

implication.text: For concurrent-flow SIBAL fabric in microgravity, the cited combined BASS/BASS-II results support treating flow near the reported low-speed quenching boundary as a regime where extinction can occur, but the boundary is conditional on oxygen level and does not establish an outcome for PMMA or a different flow direction.

The records do not support a quantitative PMMA ventilation-speed rule for the queried fabric-sheet geometry: the available PMMA outcomes concern thin films in opposed flow, while the query leaves flow speed, oxygen concentration, pressure, and thickness unspecified.

answers.question: Do solid materials burn at lower oxygen concentrations in microgravity than the NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 upward flammability test suggests?

observed.text: A NASA source reports that, in microgravity flow-tunnel tests, the 1g upward limiting oxygen index and maximum oxygen concentration were higher than the 0g values by up to 4% oxygen mole fraction; it states that the fuels burned at lower oxygen concentrations in 0g than under NASA-STD-6001 Test 1.
The BASS-II report describes a PMMA test at 22.2% ambient O2 and 5 cm/s opposed flow: flame spread was recorded, with a reported spread rate of 2.2 mm/s, and the flow was abruptly cut off.
The BASS-II report describes a PMMA test at 21% ambient O2 and 3 cm/s initial opposed flow; the recorded observation says burning was steady at 3 and 5 cm/s and the sample burned out.

implication.text: The cited comparison supports a qualified yes: some tested fuels had lower reported oxygen limits in microgravity than in the 1g upward-test comparison, but this is not evidence that every solid material does so.

The BASS-II PMMA examples show sustained burning in reported tests, including one at 21% ambient O2, but they do not establish a lower oxygen limit than Test 1 because the cited records do not provide a matched Test 1 comparison for those tests.

answers.question: How effective was a nitrogen jet at extinguishing burning solid samples in the BASS microgravity experiments?

observed.text: In BASS test BASS-3-18, the record says the N2 jet blew off the stagnation region but did not extinguish the wake flame; the wake flame remained after airflow was turned off.
In BASS test BASS-8-45, the record notes N2 extinguishment, but says the flame did not go out until the fan was reduced further; the documented terminal event is extinction at reduced flow.

BASS-3-18 and BASS-8-45 involved PMMA spheres in ISS microgravity, but their test records do not establish an N2-only extinguishing limit: BASS-3-18 ended with operator airflow shutoff, and BASS-8-45 ended after reduced-flow steps.

implication.text: The records show mixed effectiveness rather than reliable extinguishment: one test explicitly reports that the jet did not extinguish the wake, while another reports extinguishment only in a sequence that also changed airflow.

These observations do not quantify an N2-only quench threshold or establish performance across solid materials and geometries; the jet flow conditions are not reported as a quantitative dose in these records.

answers.question: Below what oxygen concentration do methanol and heptane droplets stop burning in microgravity, and how do CO2 and helium dilution change that limit?

observed.text: In microgravity droplet tests, methanol's limiting oxygen index in O2–N2–CO2 and O2–N2–He mixtures was reported as around 12% to 13% oxygen by volume; the study varied CO2 or helium dilution from 0% to 70% by volume.
The cited FLEX heptane record at 21% ambient O2 used 70% CO2 and ended in droplet disruption at 309.3 kPa; it does not establish an oxygen cutoff.
A separate FLEX heptane test at 21% ambient O2 and 70% CO2 reported hot-flame extinction at an extinction diameter of 1.77 mm, at 207.2 kPa; this is not a limiting oxygen measurement.

implication.text: The supplied evidence does not establish a heptane limiting oxygen index or quantify how CO2 versus helium changes that limit; the methanol value should not be presented as a heptane result.
Treat the reported 12% to 13% methanol LOI as applicable only to the cited microgravity droplet experiments and their oxygen–inert-gas mixtures, not as a universal fire-suppression threshold.

answers.question: What are cool flames observed in microgravity droplet combustion experiments, and why do they matter for spacecraft fire safety?

observed.text: In CFI test CFI-1206, the hot flame extinguished at a reported droplet diameter of 3.577 mm, while cool-flame burning continued at a reported burning-rate constant of 0.385 mm²/s; the record lists cool-flame extinction as the terminal event.

In CFI test CFI-1213, at 17% ambient O2, the hot flame extinguished at a reported droplet diameter of 4.113 mm and cool-flame burning continued at 0.359 mm²/s; cool-flame extinction was the terminal event.
The CFI investigation summary describes cool flames as not visible to the naked eye and reports that cool-flame-supported quasi-steady droplet burning was first observed on the ISS.

implication.text: For spacecraft fire-safety assessment, hot-flame disappearance alone is not evidence that droplet combustion has ended: the cited tests document continued cool-flame burning after hot-flame extinction.

The reported invisibility to the naked eye makes these observations relevant to considering whether visual checks alone could miss ongoing droplet combustion; the records do not establish a detector-performance result or a spacecraft safety limit.
